title: Why Your Data Dashboard Stinks
intro: A dashboard can be accurate and visually clean and still lead users to wrong conclusions. The chart being correct isn't enough — the takeaway has to be correct too.

learn.title: Five ways dashboards mislead
learn.text:
Tufte's principles (data-ink ratio, avoid chartjunk) address how a chart is **presented** — not how people **perceive** it.

1. **Misleading continuity** — Lines connect unrelated snapshots, implying a trend that doesn't exist.

2. **Accidental grouping** — Proximity and shared color make users infer relationships between unrelated metrics.

3. **Color assumptions** — Users read red/green/yellow as bad/good/average. Colorblindness and cultural differences make it worse. Color should never be the only signal.

4. **Memory overload** — Toggles and tabs force users to remember values across screens instead of comparing directly. (Nielsen: recognition rather than recall.)

5. **Anchoring and framing** — The first metric shown becomes the benchmark. 'Risk' vs. 'Stability' changes emotional response to the same number.

try.q: A dashboard shows revenue and headcount on the same line chart with dual Y-axes. Both go up. What will users likely conclude?
options: That revenue and headcount are related — even if they're not
That revenue is more important because it's on the left
Nothing — dual Y-axes are clear
That both metrics are performing well
try.explain: Proximity + shared chart = accidental grouping. Users infer correlation from co-location, even when there is none.

learn.title: Start from the decision, not the data
learn.text:
Most dashboards start with: "What data do we have?" then display all of it.

The right question: **"What decision does the user need to make?"**

Then show only the data that supports that decision.

A sales manager looking at pipeline doesn't need 15 charts. They need to know:
→ Am I on track to hit quota?
→ Which deals need attention this week?
→ What changed since last week?

Three questions. Maybe four charts. Everything else is noise.

try.q: A PM asks you to 'add user engagement metrics to the dashboard.' What do you ask first?
options: What decision will these metrics help someone make?
Which chart type should we use?
How many metrics do we have?
Where should they go on the page?
try.explain: Start from the decision. If a metric doesn't support a specific decision, it's just noise on the screen.

learn.title: Practical fixes
learn.text:
**Show comparisons side by side** — not behind toggles or tabs. Users can't accurately compare values they have to remember.

**Use inline labels and direct annotations** — not separate legends. Every legend lookup is a micro-interruption.

**Add context** — benchmarks, thresholds, previous-period values. A number without context has no meaning. '12%' means nothing. '12%, up from 8%, target is 15%' tells a story.

**State scope explicitly** — timeframe, population, and scope in titles, sublabels, and tooltips.

**Pair color with shape, text, or position** — color alone fails for colorblindness and grayscale printing.

**Give KPIs equal visual weight** — unless you intentionally want to anchor on one.

try.q: A KPI card shows '94%' with no other context. What's missing?
options: Comparison point — previous period, target, or benchmark
A chart showing the trend
The exact number of users
A color indicator
try.explain: '94%' means nothing alone. Is it up or down? Is 94% good or bad? A benchmark or previous value gives meaning.

test.q: What's the core problem with most dashboards?
options: They can be accurate and clean but still lead users to wrong conclusions
They use too many colors
They show too little data
They aren't updated frequently enough
test.explain: If the chart is correct but the takeaway is wrong, the work is not finished. Perception matters as much as accuracy.

test.q: What does 'anchoring' mean in dashboard design?
options: The first metric shown becomes the benchmark users compare everything else against
Pinning a chart to the top of the page
Using a fixed Y-axis scale
Keeping the same layout across dashboard versions
test.explain: Anchoring bias: whatever users see first sets their frame of reference. This means the order and prominence of metrics matters.

test.q: Why are toggles and tabs bad for data comparison?
options: They force users to remember values across screens instead of comparing directly
They add too many clicks
They slow down page load
They're not accessible
test.explain: Recognition rather than recall (Nielsen). Humans are bad at remembering exact values. Show comparisons side by side.

test.q: What question should you ask FIRST when designing a dashboard?
options: What decision does the user need to make?
What data is available?
What chart types work best?
How many KPIs should we show?
test.explain: Decision-first design. The user's decision determines what data to show. Everything else is noise.

test.q: Why should color never be the only differentiator in a chart?
options: Colorblindness, cultural differences, and grayscale printing all break color-only encoding
Colors don't look good on all screens
Users prefer shapes over colors
Color is harder to implement in code
test.explain: ~8% of men have some form of colorblindness. Pair color with shape, text, or position. Color reinforces — it shouldn't carry the signal alone.
